title: Gold doubles in a year as inflation passes 12 percent
what: Gold averaged 455 dollars an ounce in December, 16 percent more than in November and more than twice its price of a year ago. Consumer prices in November were 12.6 percent higher than a year earlier. Since the Federal Reserve under its new chairman Paul Volcker said on 6 October that it would control the supply of money rather than steer interest rates, the rate banks charge each other has run near 14 percent. The numbers: the Fed's rate 13.8 percent. Inflation 12.6 percent. Unemployment 5.9 percent.
why: The opening position of the game: double-digit inflation, a Fed that has just changed course, and gold in a speculative run that peaks a month later. Every rates story of the next forty years starts from here.

title: Gold hits a record above 840 dollars
what: On 21 January the London gold fixing reached a record 843 dollars an ounce, three days after silver touched 49.45 dollars. Gold averaged 675 dollars in January, almost half as much again as in December. Buyers want metal instead of money after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, with American hostages still held in Tehran and consumer prices 13.3 percent higher in December than a year earlier.
why: The top of gold's 1970s bull market. The January 1980 monthly average was not seen again until May 2006, and in real terms not for decades: the game's starkest lesson about buying at the peak of a panic.

title: The Fed's rate tumbles from 17.6 to 9.5 percent; bonds and gold bounce back
what: Interest rates are falling as fast as they rose. The Fed's interest rate, the rate at which banks lend to each other, averaged under 9.5 percent in June against 17.6 percent in April, because the economy is in recession. When rates fall, existing bonds become more valuable, because they still promise the old, higher return: the US Treasury 2000, which lost a third of its value in the first three months of the year, has gained almost 60 percent since the end of March, 8 percent of it in June, and is worth more again than at New Year. Gold rebounded and averaged 601 dollars, 17 percent more than in May. The numbers: the Fed's rate 9.5 percent. Inflation 14.4 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: Volcker's first squeeze ends in retreat: the Fed lets rates drop with the recession, and gold and long bond yields start rising again over the summer. Inflation was not yet beaten, which is why the second squeeze in the autumn had to be harder. The Treasury 2000 is down 23% since December 1979 (13.09 to 10.11), so the year-to-date figure the curator asked for is negative; the beat gives it together with the rebound since March. The article should mention the 2000 vintage bond price return ytd from the game."]

title: The Fed drives its interest rate to 19 percent
what: The Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker fights inflation by making money expensive. Its interest rate, the rate at which banks lend to each other, averaged nearly 19 percent in December; in July it was 9.0 percent. Banks pass this on to their customers: even the best ones now pay 21.5 percent for a loan. Gold averaged 538 dollars, 14 percent less than in November. The numbers: the Fed's rate 18.9 percent. Inflation 12.6 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: The defining number of the Volcker era. Money in a savings account now beats gold and shares on interest alone, and gold's twenty-year bear market has effectively begun.

title: The Fed holds its rate at 19 percent and gold slides below 410
what: The Federal Reserve has held its interest rate near 19 percent since May, as high as it has ever been. Consumer prices in June were 9.6 percent higher than a year earlier, so lenders now earn far more than inflation takes away, and saving pays better than owning gold. Gold averaged 409 dollars in July, 11 percent below June and the lowest since November 1979. The numbers: the Fed's rate 19.0 percent. Inflation 9.6 percent. Unemployment 7.5 percent.
why: This is what 'real rates' mean in practice: a 10-point gap between interest and inflation. Gold has lost almost 40 percent from its January 1980 average and keeps falling.

title: The Fed's rate eases to 16 percent, but lending for ten years costs more than ever
what: The Fed's interest rate fell to just under 16 percent in September, from 19 percent in the summer. But investors who lend their money for ten years still demand more than ever before: the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds averaged 15.3 percent, against about 11.5 percent a year ago, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 18.4 percent. The S&P 500 lost 5 percent in the month as the economy weakens. Shares of companies whose profits lie far in the future, or that depend on borrowing, fell hardest: Apple Computer lost 24 percent, Sony 15, Schlumberger 14 and Intel 13, while steady earners such as McDonald's and Coca-Cola rose. The numbers: the Fed's rate 15.9 percent. Inflation 10.8 percent. Unemployment 7.4 percent.
why: The all-time high in long-term US interest rates and the low point for bond prices. Anyone who locked in these yields made the trade of a lifetime: the great bond bull market starts from here, though nobody could know it this month. title: Gold falls to 330 dollars as inflation retreats
what: Gold averaged 330 dollars in March, 12 percent below February, the lowest since August 1979 and less than half its January 1980 average. Inflation has dropped to 7.6 percent (February) while the rate banks charge each other is near 15 percent, so money in the bank earns about 7 percent more than prices rise. The prime rate stands at 16.5 percent.
why: Gold's first bottom of the Volcker years. Falling inflation plus very high interest rates is the worst combination for a metal that pays nothing.

title: Gold jumps 20 percent as rates fall and Mexico wobbles
what: Gold averaged 437 dollars in September, 20 percent more than in August and almost 40 percent above its June average. Falling interest rates make gold cheaper to hold, and Mexico's announcement in August that it cannot pay its foreign debts has raised fears for the banks that lent to it. Ten-year Treasury yields averaged 12.3 percent, down from 14.3 percent in June.
why: A sharp counter-rally inside gold's long decline, driven by the same rate cuts that lit the stock market. It fades within months.

title: Gold slumps after OPEC cuts the oil price
what: Gold averaged 420 dollars in March, 14 percent below February's 491. On 14 March OPEC cut its base oil price from 34 to 29 dollars a barrel, the first cut in its history, after twelve days of talks. US inflation is down to 3.5 percent (February), and the rate banks charge each other is still near 8.75 percent.
why: Cheaper oil removes the last inflation scare that had lifted gold since the summer. From here gold drifts lower for two years.

title: The Fed raises rates for the first time in five years
what: On 4 February the Federal Reserve raised its target for the rate banks charge each other from 3 to 3.25 percent, its first increase since 1989. Long-term rates had come a long way down: the 10-year Treasury yield averaged 5.3 percent last October, against 15.3 percent in September 1981. Bond prices fell: the 30-year Treasury yield, 6.17 percent on 12 January, and the 10-year yield, which averaged 5.75 percent in January, are both rising. Inflation is only about 2.5 percent (January). The numbers: the Fed's rate 3.25 percent. Inflation 2.5 percent. Unemployment 6.6 percent.
why: The first shot of the 1994 bond massacre. Greenspan moved before inflation showed up, a pre-emptive strike that hurt bondholders badly in 1994 but set up the long boom of the late 1990s.

title: Sixth hike of the year as bond losses mount
what: On 15 November the Fed raised its rate target by three quarters of a point to 5.5 percent, its sixth increase this year, and banks raised the prime rate to 8.5 percent. The 30-year Treasury yield reached 8.16 percent on 4 November, up from 6.17 percent in January. Inflation is still under 3 percent, yet a 16-year zero-coupon Treasury has lost about 14 percent of its value this year. In November itself long-term bonds steadied: the US Treasury 2010 gained 2 percent. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.5 percent. Inflation 2.6 percent. Unemployment 5.8 percent.
why: The worst year for bonds in decades, with global losses later put at about 1.5 trillion dollars, and the backdrop to the Mexican peso crisis. Rates peaked in early 1995 and the bond rally that followed was enormous.

title: Britain will sell half its gold
what: On 7 May the British government said it would sell about 395 tonnes of gold, roughly half its reserves, in auctions from July; gold stood at 282.40 dollars that day. Gold averaged 276 dollars in May, its lowest monthly average since 1979. With inflation around 2 percent (April) and shares booming, few investors want a metal that pays nothing.
why: The emblem of gold's twenty-year bear market. The price bottomed at 252.80 dollars on 20 July, in the month the auctions began; 'Brown's bottom' became a byword for selling at the low.

title: Europe's central banks agree to limit gold sales, and gold jumps
what: On 26 September fifteen European central banks agreed in Washington to sell no more than about 400 tonnes of gold a year, 2,000 tonnes over five years, and not to expand their gold lending. The price jumped: gold averaged 311 dollars in October, 17 percent above September and up from a 20-year low of 252.80 dollars on 20 July.
why: The floor under gold's long decline. The price sagged once more in 2001, but the Washington Agreement marks the end of the bear market and the start of the long rise of the 2000s.

title: The Fed cuts by half a point, twice in one month
what: On 3 January, in an unscheduled move, the Fed cut its rate target by half a point to 6 percent, citing weakening sales and production, falling consumer confidence and high energy prices. At its meeting at the end of the month it cut by another half point, to 5.5 percent. As recently as May 2000 it had raised the rate to 6.5 percent to cool the boom. The surprise cut sent the Nasdaq up 14.17% that day, its biggest gain ever, and 12% over the month; beaten-down technology shares rebounded hardest, with Microsoft up about 41% in January and Apple 45%. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.5 percent. Inflation 3.4 percent. Unemployment 3.9 percent.
why: The start of the 2001 easing: eleven cuts in one year took the rate to 1.75 percent, but could not stop the dot-com bust or the recession.

title: The Fed's rate falls to 1 percent
what: On 25 June the Fed cut its rate target by a quarter point to 1 percent, the lowest since the 1950s; since January 2001 it has cut thirteen times from 6.5 percent. Inflation is about 2.1 percent (May). The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 3.3 percent in June, the lowest since 1958, and a 30-year mortgage costs about 5.2 percent, the lowest since the mortgage company Freddie Mac began its weekly survey in 1971. The numbers: the Fed's rate 1 percent. Inflation 2.1 percent. Unemployment 6.1 percent.
why: Rock-bottom rates fuelled the housing boom that ended in 2008. Long bond yields bottomed in June 2003 and jumped by more than a point within weeks, a sharp loss for latecomers to the bond rally.

title: Bond prices tumble as yields jump: the 2020 Treasury loses 14% in a month
what: In mid-June yields on US government bonds were at a 45-year low, because investors expected the Fed to cut its rate by half a point and perhaps even to buy long-term bonds itself to keep yields down. The Fed cut by only a quarter point on 25 June, and on 15 July Alan Greenspan told Congress that there are signs of recovery and that such special measures are 'most unlikely' to be needed. The yield on 10-year Treasuries leapt from 3.13 percent on 13 June to 4.49 percent on 31 July, the sharpest rise since 1994, made worse by investors in mortgage securities, who sell Treasuries to protect themselves when rates rise. A bond pays a fixed amount of interest, so when new bonds offer more, existing ones are worth less, and the longer a bond still runs, the more it loses: in July the Treasury due in 2005 hardly moved, the one due in 2010 fell 6% and the one due in 2020 fell 14%. A 30-year mortgage now costs about 5.9 percent, up from 5.2 percent in June. The numbers: the Fed's rate 1 percent. Inflation 2.1 percent. Unemployment 6.3 percent.
why: One month after the story about the lowest yields since 1958, the player learns the other side: a 'safe' long bond can lose 14% in a month when yields rise, while a short one barely moves. The sell-off ended the deflation scare, and mortgage rates did not return to the June 2003 low until the financial crisis.

title: Greenspan's 'conundrum': long rates fall while the Fed raises
what: Since June 2004 the Fed has raised its rate target in quarter-point steps from 1 to 2.5 percent, yet long-term rates have fallen: the 10-year Treasury yield averaged about 4.2 percent in February against 4.7 percent last June. On 16 February Alan Greenspan told Congress that the behaviour of world bond markets 'remains a conundrum'. The numbers: the Fed's rate 2.5 percent. Inflation 3.0 percent. Unemployment 5.3 percent.
why: Cheap long-term money, partly from Asian savings flowing into Treasuries, kept mortgage rates low and the housing bubble inflating even as the Fed tightened.

title: Gold passes 600 dollars for the first time since 1980, up 10% in April
what: On 11 April gold rose above 600 dollars an ounce for the first time since 1980; it has doubled in four years. The same day copper passed 6,000 dollars a tonne, a record, and silver reached its highest in 23 years: investment funds are buying metals as an alternative to shares, bonds and a dollar they expect to weaken. Tension over Iran's nuclear programme added to the rush; later in the month oil set a record above 73 dollars a barrel and gold touched 640 dollars. Gold averaged 611 dollars in April, 10 percent more than in March.
why: The steepest stretch of gold's climb in the commodity boom of 2003 to 2008: gold rose 10% in April and another 10% in May, to its highest monthly average since January 1980, before falling back in June (told in the June 2006 story). It shows the boom as a rush of investment money into all commodities at once, not only China's demand for copper.

title: Seventeenth hike in a row; gold falls back from a 26-year high
what: On 29 June the Fed raised its rate target to 5.25 percent, its seventeenth quarter-point increase since June 2004, under Ben Bernanke, chairman since 1 February. Gold, which averaged 675 dollars in May, its highest since January 1980, fell back to an average of 596 dollars in June, 12 percent less. Inflation was 4.2 percent in May. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.25 percent. Inflation 4.2 percent. Unemployment 4.6 percent.
why: The end of the Greenspan-Bernanke tightening and a first test of gold's new bull market, which shrugged off the drop and passed 800 dollars within eighteen months.

title: Zero interest rates and the Fed starts buying bonds
what: On 16 December the Fed cut its rate target to a range of 0 to 0.25 percent, the lowest ever, and said rates would stay exceptionally low 'for some time'. In January 1981 the same rate had averaged 19 percent. On 25 November it had announced it would buy up to 500 billion dollars of mortgage bonds and 100 billion of mortgage-agency debt, and it is considering buying Treasury bonds as well. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 2.4 percent in December, and consumer prices in November were only 1.1 percent higher than a year earlier. Long Treasury bonds gained about a quarter in November and December. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0 to 0.25 percent. Inflation 1.1 percent. Unemployment 6.8 percent.
why: The beginning of zero rates and quantitative easing, which lasted seven years and shaped every asset price until 2022. Long bonds gained while almost everything else fell.

title: Money is free: the Fed creates a trillion dollars to buy bonds
what: The Fed's interest rate has been at zero since December: banks can borrow almost for free. Because a rate cannot go much lower than zero, the Fed now uses another tool. On 18 March it said it would buy another 750 billion dollars of mortgage bonds and, for the first time, 300 billion dollars of government bonds, with money it creates itself. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0 to 0.25 percent. Inflation 0.2 percent. Unemployment 8.3 percent.
why: The start of the age of free money. Buying bonds pushes long-term rates down too; the practice is called quantitative easing.

title: Gold passes 1,000 dollars again as the dollar weakens
what: On 8 September gold rose above 1,000 dollars an ounce for the first time since February, its highest since March 2008, when it set a record a little above 1,030 dollars; the dollar weakened and the euro rose to about 1.45 dollars. With interest rates near zero in many large economies it costs little to hold gold, which pays no interest, and on 23 September the Fed repeated that its rate would stay exceptionally low 'for an extended period'. Gold averaged 997 dollars in September, 5 percent more than in August. Shares rose too: on 15 September, a year after Lehman's bankruptcy, Fed chairman Ben Bernanke said the recession was 'very likely over', though unemployment stood at 9.7 percent, a 26-year high, and the S&P 500 gained 4% in the month to 1,057.08.
why: The start of gold's second leg: it passed its 2008 record in October 2009 and kept rising until 2011, driven by zero rates and distrust of the dollar. The Bernanke remark of 15 September marks the official mood a year after Lehman; the recession was later dated as having ended in June 2009.

what: By 16 August the S&P 500 had risen more than 17 percent from its June low, on hopes that the Fed would soon change course. On 26 August, at the Kansas City Fed's symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Fed chairman Jerome Powell dashed them: bringing inflation down would require high rates 'for some time' and would 'bring some pain to households and businesses', and history 'cautions strongly against prematurely loosening policy'. The S&P 500 fell 3.4 percent that day and ended August down 4 percent at 3,955.00. The 10-year Treasury yield rose from 2.67 percent at the end of July to 3.15 percent, and because bond prices fall when yields rise, the Treasury bond due in 2040 lost 6 percent. title: Silicon Valley Bank fails on its bond losses
what: On 8 March Silicon Valley Bank said it had sold over 21 billion dollars of bonds at a loss of 1.8 billion; customers withdrew 42 billion dollars the next day, and on 10 March regulators seized the bank, which had 209 billion dollars of assets. The bonds had lost value as interest rates rose. The authorities created a new lending facility for banks, and short-term Treasury yields fell sharply. On 22 March the Fed still raised its rate by a quarter point to 4.75 to 5 percent. Signature Bank failed two days later and regional bank shares fell sharply, but the S&P 500 ended March up 4 percent. In the panic investors fled into government bonds, and their prices rose although the Fed raised its rate once more: the US Treasury 2040 gained almost 6 percent in March. The numbers: the Fed's rate 4.75 to 5 percent. Inflation 6.0 percent. Unemployment 3.6 percent.
why: The bill for the fastest hikes in forty years: bonds bought at near-zero yields sank, and a bank run followed. It marked the beginning of the end of the hiking cycle.

title: The Fed pencils in three rate cuts and long bonds gain 10 percent
what: On 13 December the Fed left its rate at 5.25 to 5.5 percent for the third meeting in a row, and its members' projections put the rate at 4.6 percent at the end of 2024, which means three quarter-point cuts; in September they had still expected 5.1 percent. Chairman Jerome Powell said the Fed was 'likely at or near the peak rate for this cycle', and traders bet on about twice as many cuts as the Fed projects. The 10-year Treasury yield, 4.98 percent on 19 October, fell below 4 percent on 14 December for the first time since July and ended the year at 3.88 percent. When yields fall, the prices of existing bonds rise, long-dated ones most: the Treasury bond due in 2040 gained 10 percent in December, after 9 percent in November. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.25 to 5.5 percent. Inflation 3.1 percent. Unemployment 3.7 percent.
why: The Fed's turn of December 2023 crowned the best two months for long bonds in the game's recent years (the 2040 Treasury +9% and +10%). The cuts came later and fewer than traders bet (the first in September 2024), which explains the bond setbacks of early 2024, such as April's 7% loss.

title: Gold passes 2,400 dollars, up 8 percent in a month
what: Gold rose above 2,300 dollars an ounce for the first time in the first days of April and above 2,400 on 12 April, as Israel braced for an attack by Iran; it averaged 2,331 dollars in April, 8 percent more than in March and 15 percent more than in February. It climbed although the dollar is strong and hopes of early interest-rate cuts in America have faded, which would normally weigh on a metal that pays no interest. The World Gold Council points to buyers in Asia and to central banks, which added 290 tonnes in the first quarter, the most in a first quarter since its figures begin in 2000; China's central bank has reported purchases for 17 months in a row.
why: The start of gold's rise from about 2,000 dollars to above 4,000 in 2025: in spring 2024 it stopped following American interest rates and the dollar, carried by central banks (China's above all) and Asian buyers. Prepares the gold stories of September 2024 and after.
